# 1 Clement Chapter 4 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)

**Translator:** SOPHIA | **Source:** Codex Alexandrinus, 1 Clement 4 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-EC/1CL_004_page_001.jpg

---

## Council Notes

Chapter 4 opens Clement's extended catena on jealousy (*zelos*) — an anti-virtue catalogue drawn from scripture. Each verse presents a biblical case: Cain (full LXX quotation), Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Aaron/Miriam, Dathan/Abiram, David. The chapter leads directly to chapter 5's pivot to Christian examples (Peter and Paul). The phrase "our father Jacob" is notable — Clement, writing to Gentile Christians, uses the patriarchal "our," claiming the Jewish story as the church's own.

The LXX quotation of Genesis 4 in vv.1-3 is close to but not identical to standard LXX. Agents agree on the rendering of the murder itself (v.3). Main disagreements concern: (1) Gen 4:7's notoriously difficult text; (2) "sold into slavery" vs. "sold into bondage" for Joseph; (3) structure of the refrain.

The Gen 4:7 rendering is famously obscure. The LXX reads *hēsuchason, pros se hē apostrophē autou, kai su arxeis autou* — "Be at peace; to you is his turning, and you shall rule over him." SOPHIA preserves this literalistically since it mirrors the curse of Gen 3:16.

---

## Chapter 4

**4:1** For it is written thus: "And it came to pass after certain days that Cain brought from the fruits of the earth a sacrifice to God, and Abel also brought from the firstborn of his flock and from their fat portions. And God looked upon Abel and his gifts, but upon Cain and upon his sacrifices he did not look. And Cain was very sorrowful and his face fell." [Gen 4:3-5 LXX]

**4:2** "And God said to Cain: 'Why are you very sorrowful and why has your face fallen? If you offered rightly but did not divide rightly, did you not sin? Be still; his turning is toward you, and you shall rule over him.'" [Gen 4:6-7 LXX]

**4:3** "And Cain said to Abel his brother: 'Let us go into the field.' And it came to pass when they were in the field that Cain rose up against Abel his brother and killed him." [Gen 4:8 LXX]

**4:4** You see, brothers, jealousy and envy wrought a fratricide.

**4:5** On account of jealousy our father Jacob fled from the face of his brother Esau. [Gen 27:41ff]

**4:6** Jealousy caused Joseph to be persecuted and sold into bondage. [Gen 37]

**4:7** Jealousy compelled Moses to flee from the face of Pharaoh king of Egypt, when he heard from his own kinsman: "Who made you a ruler and a judge over us? Do you wish to slay me as you slew the Egyptian yesterday?" [Exod 2:14 LXX]

**4:8** On account of jealousy Aaron and Miriam were lodged outside the camp. [Num 12:14-15]

**4:9** Jealousy sent Dathan and Abiram down alive into Hades, because they raised sedition against Moses the servant of God. [Num 16:33]

**4:10** On account of jealousy David not only met with envy from foreigners but also endured persecution from Saul king of Israel. [1 Sam 18:6ff]

---

*SOPHIA consensus translation. Completed 2026-03-17.*
